title: MAS Proposes Tougher Technology Risk Notices for Insurers, Banks and Other Firms: Asset Inventories, Immutable Backups and Counting Partial Outages Toward the Four-Hour Downtime Limit
summary: MAS consulted until July 31, 2026 on amendments to its Technology Risk Management Notices covering insurers, banks, payment firms and others, proposing IT asset inventories, risk registers, capacity planning, change management, continuous monitoring, immutable or offline backups, and counting partial or intermittent disruption toward the four-hour annual downtime limit.
description:
Singapore's financial regulator wants regulated firms to tighten how they manage technology risk, from the way they track their systems to how they back up data and count outages. According to an analysis by the law firm Rajah & Tann Asia dated July 17, 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) consulted on amendments to its Notices on Technology Risk Management, inviting submissions by July 31, 2026. The proposed requirements would take effect 12 months after the finalised Notices are published, so firms would have a year to adapt.

The Notices apply to a wide range of institutions. The Rajah & Tann article lists the current framework as covering licensed insurers (Notice FSM-N03), banks, credit card or charge card licensees, finance companies, merchant banks, payment system operators, settlement institutions and digital payment token service licensees, licensed credit bureaus, registered insurance brokers, capital markets institutions, licensed financial advisers and licensed trust companies. The article lists FSM-N03 as applicable but does not say how the proposals affect insurers differently from other institutions.

The proposals touch several areas. On IT asset management, firms would keep a current inventory of IT assets, including hardware, software, cryptographic assets, open-source components and third-party components. A complete inventory is the basis for knowing what needs patching or replacing, and the inclusion of cryptographic and open-source assets reflects concerns about hidden dependencies. On risk assessment and monitoring, firms would carry out regular assessments and mitigate risks in proportion to their severity, maintain a risk register listing material risks, risk owners and mitigation measures, and track key risk indicators. The article links this to supply-chain and AI-related threats.

Capacity planning is another proposal: critical systems, and the systems they depend on, should have enough capacity for business needs, growth and surges in customer traffic. Change management rules would require firms to prevent unauthorised changes, assess change risks before implementation, including upstream and downstream effects, test changes to critical systems and have recovery measures ready. Firms would monitor critical systems continuously, with defined alert thresholds and response procedures.

Backups receive particular attention. Firms would keep immutable or offline backups of data that is crucial to business services. Immutable backups cannot be altered or deleted once written, and offline backups are disconnected from the network, so both protect against ransomware that encrypts or destroys data. For incident management, firms would define roles and responsibilities, preserve evidence, communicate with stakeholders and customers, and promptly notify senior management.

One proposal concerns the way downtime is counted. The current framework limits unscheduled downtime to four hours per critical system in any 12-month period. MAS proposes that partial or intermittent disruptions count toward this total. In practical terms, a system that is slow, available to only some customers or repeatedly dropping would use up part of the allowance even if it never fully stops, which closes a gap that might otherwise let firms report systems as "up" while customers struggle.

MAS asks nine consultation questions. Among them, according to the article, are whether backups should be both immutable and offline, whether backup frequency should be prescribed, and whether the term "partial or intermittent disruption" is clear enough. Those questions show where the regulator expects debate: how prescriptive the rules should be, and how to define a partial outage objectively.

The article is explicit about what it does not cover. It does not describe incident reporting timelines to MAS, recovery time objectives, or specific outsourcing and third-party requirements, other than mentioning supply-chain risk in the context of risk assessment. Readers who need those details should consult the full consultation paper.

The proposals come at a time of growing concern about concentration in technology services. A recent outage of Google Cloud's London region disrupted UK banking services on October 20, 2026, and shows how a single provider's failure can spread. The Singapore proposals do not mention that event, which happened after the consultation closed, but they address the same question, how firms can keep critical services running when technology fails, and they require firms to understand and monitor their dependencies.

It is also worth noting how the Notices relate to the rest of the regulatory system. MAS already sets technology risk expectations in guidelines, and the Notices make certain requirements binding. Because the same Notice family covers banks, payment firms, insurers, brokers and advisers, a change in one place affects very different businesses: a large bank with hundreds of critical systems and a small insurance broker with a handful. The consultation's questions on how prescriptive to be, for example on backup frequency, reflect the difficulty of writing rules that are meaningful for the largest firms and proportionate for the smallest. Industry responses, which were due by July 31, will show how much flexibility firms seek.

What should firms do? Compliance teams will want to review their asset inventories and confirm they capture cryptographic and third-party components, check that backups meet the immutability or offline standard, and revisit how they measure downtime. Because the effective date is 12 months after publication of the final Notices, there is time to plan, but the final text may differ from the proposals in light of feedback. For customers, the aim is more dependable digital services. For the industry, the cost is more documentation, testing and monitoring, which may fall more heavily on smaller firms.
source_name: Rajah & Tann Asia (analysis dated July 17, 2026) and Monetary Authority of Singapore

key_points: MAS invited feedback on proposed amendments to its Technology Risk Management Notices by July 31, 2026; the revised requirements would take effect 12 months after the finalised Notices are published.

The Notices cover licensed insurers (FSM-N03), banks, card issuers, finance companies, merchant banks, payment system operators, credit bureaus, insurance brokers, capital markets institutions, financial advisers and trust companies.

Proposals include a current IT asset inventory (covering cryptographic, open-source and third-party components), a risk register with key risk indicators, capacity planning, stricter change management and continuous monitoring of critical systems.
Firms would keep immutable or offline backups of data crucial to business services, with defined incident-management roles, evidence preservation and prompt notification of senior management.

The current limit of four hours of unscheduled downtime per critical system in any 12-month period would count partial or intermittent disruptions toward the total; MAS asks nine consultation questions.
why_it_matters: Insurers, banks and payment firms depend on technology that customers cannot do without. Tighter rules on backups, change control and downtime are meant to make outages and cyberattacks less damaging, and could mean extra compliance work and costs for regulated firms in Singapore.

title: Bank of Canada Says the Financial System Held Up Against Tariffs and Geopolitical Shocks but Flags Stretched Households, Highest Insolvencies Since 2009 and a 15% Payment Rise on Pandemic-Era Mortgages
summary: The Bank of Canada's May 28, 2026 Financial Stability Report says households, businesses and banks have remained stable, with shocks less widespread than feared, while warning that heavily indebted households have little room to absorb a shock, insolvencies are the highest since 2009 and pandemic-era mortgages face payment rises of about 15%.
description:
The Bank of Canada has told Canadians that the financial system has coped well with a turbulent year, while making clear that the comfort is not evenly shared. According to BNN Bloomberg on May 28, 2026, the central bank's financial stability report, a 42-page document, concludes that the system has held up despite United States tariffs, rising geopolitical risk and uncertainty linked to artificial intelligence. The bank says the effects of these shocks have been narrower than it had expected, and the report states that the impacts have been less widespread than was initially feared. Canadian households and businesses have remained stable, and banks have strengthened their ability to absorb shocks. Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers acknowledged that the data look better than many people's lived experience, saying that it can be true that the data look better and people still feel stressed.

The report is specific about where the strain lies. Many households carry high debt relative to income, which leaves them exposed to job loss or a large unexpected expense. According to Canadian Mortgage Professional, Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle said households with the highest debt burdens have very little financial flexibility to cope with a job loss or an unexpected expense, and he noted that some households face far greater strain than others. The household debt to disposable income ratio has risen slightly over the past year but remains below its 2022 peak, and Rogers said Canadians have saved a bit more and paid down some debt in recent years. Overall household wealth has risen and mortgage delinquency rates have stabilised, but the averages hide pressure on many borrowers. Rogers also said some households have not gained enough wealth to offset higher living costs. The coverage does not report debt service ratios, unemployment or a specific delinquency rate, so those measures are not given here.

Insolvency data show the stress most plainly. BNN Bloomberg reported that Equifax Canada data show insolvencies at their highest level since 2009, up 18.8 per cent year over year, which the report links to inflation. The report says many consumers may have reached a financial inflection point. Canadian Mortgage Professional added that Equifax Canada's Kathy Catsiliras said rising mortgage renewals and debt pressure are pushing more homeowners toward consumer proposals, a formal arrangement for repaying debts at a reduced amount. A licensed mortgage broker quoted in the same article, Zlatkin of LowestRates.ca, said the pressure on homeowners is real.

Mortgage renewals are the mechanism through which the central bank sees the next phase of stress. Mortgages taken out during the pandemic, when rates were very low, are coming up for renewal at higher rates. BNN Bloomberg reported that these loans make up about 12 per cent of outstanding mortgages, that they are due for renewal within the next 12 months, and that borrowers in this group are expected to see payments rise by about 15 per cent on average. A payment rise of 15 per cent on, for illustration, a monthly payment of $2,000 would add about $300 a month, which is simple arithmetic and not a figure from the report. Canadian Mortgage Professional reported that the bank expects the final wave of pandemic-era renewals to be completed by the second half of 2027, which indicates that the pressure continues beyond the 12-month window cited by BNN Bloomberg. The coverage does not give the number of loans involved.

Beyond households, the report lists risks that could interact. Rogers said that vulnerabilities have increased in some parts of the system and that several could materialise together in a shock. Canadian Mortgage Professional reported that elevated equity valuations, rising corporate debt and growing hedge fund leverage in sovereign debt markets were named as risks that compound in a crisis. Geopolitical pressures were cited, including the Middle East conflict and uncertainty around the review of the Canada-United States-Mexico trade agreement. Artificial intelligence was flagged as an emerging systemic risk, mainly through more sophisticated cyberattacks. That point connects to the cyber insurance debate, since a systemic event involving widely used technology could produce losses across many sectors at once.

What does this mean for insurers? The report is a statement about banks and borrowers, not about insurers, and the coverage reviewed does not discuss the insurance sector. Even so, household stress matters to the industry. When budgets are tight, customers may shop for cheaper cover, raise deductibles or let policies lapse, and an increase in consumer proposals and insolvencies can reduce the ability of some customers to pay premiums. Insurers also invest in mortgages, corporate debt and equities, so the risks the Bank lists, valuations and corporate leverage, are relevant to their portfolios. Those links are general observations and are not drawn from the report itself.

The message of the report is balanced. The system is working, and the central bank sees no immediate threat to its stability; the data are better than the mood. But it also warns of vulnerabilities that have grown in parts of the system, and that a combination of shocks could test it. For policymakers, the focus is on the households most exposed to renewal shocks and job losses. For lenders, it is on the quality of loans written in the pandemic years. For insurers and brokers, it is on how customers behave when their budgets are stretched.

What to watch is the Bank of Canada's next financial stability publication, the pace of mortgage renewals through 2027, insolvency data from Equifax Canada and Statistics Canada, and any change in household debt ratios. The central bank's judgement that the impacts have been less widespread than feared will be tested as the last pandemic-era mortgages reset.
source_name: BNN Bloomberg (May 28, 2026) and Canadian Mortgage Professional (May 28, 2026), reporting the Bank of Canada's 2026 Financial Stability Report
image_alt: Financial district skyline representing financial system stability (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Canada's 2026 Financial Stability Report, released May 28, concludes that the financial system has held up despite US tariffs, rising geopolitical risk and uncertainty linked to artificial intelligence, saying the impacts have been less widespread than initially feared.

Households and businesses have remained stable and banks have strengthened their ability to absorb shocks, but the most heavily indebted households have very little financial flexibility to cope with a job loss or an unexpected expense.

Equifax Canada data cited in the coverage show insolvencies at their highest level since 2009, up 18.8% year over year, and the report says many consumers may have reached a financial inflection point.

Pandemic-era mortgages make up about 12% of outstanding mortgages and are due for renewal within 12 months, with payments expected to rise by about 15% on average; the final wave of such renewals is expected to finish in the second half of 2027.

The Bank named elevated equity valuations, rising corporate debt and hedge fund leverage in sovereign debt markets as risks that could compound in a crisis, and flagged AI as an emerging systemic risk mainly through more sophisticated cyberattacks.
why_it_matters: Insurers, banks and lenders in Canada all depend on households continuing to meet payments. The central bank is saying that the system is sound overall while the strain is concentrated in highly indebted households, which is where mortgage renewals and insolvencies are showing up. For insurers, the same stress can affect lapse rates, premium affordability and credit and mortgage-related investments.
